“Don’t touch that file.”
That’s what the outgoing developer told me during handover. He pointed at a file called utils.js. It was 1,847 lines long. No comments. Functions with names like doTheThing(), handler2(), and my personal favorite: fixedFinalV3().
“Why?” I asked.
He shrugged. “Nobody knows what’s in there anymore. It works. Just don’t touch it.”
I should have listened.
Six weeks later, I touched it. A small change — add a parameter to one function. The parameter rippled through eleven other functions I didn’t know existed. Three of them called each other recursively in ways I still don’t fully understand. The feature shipped, broke something else, got rolled back, and I spent two days piecing together what had happened.
That was the moment I made a decision: this codebase needed a refactor. Not a rewrite — a careful, systematic refactor. The kind where you improve the code without breaking the behavior.
What followed was four months of the most educational work I’ve done as a developer. I touched roughly 10,000 lines across 47 files. Found bugs that had been quietly living in production for over a year. Deleted more than 3,000 lines of code that were doing absolutely nothing. Improved test coverage from 23% to 71%.
And I learned things that no tutorial ever taught me.

Generated by AuthorThe Scale of the Problem (It’s Not Just Us)
Before I get into what I did, let me put this in context. Legacy code and technical debt aren’t a niche problem.
A 2025 CAST report analyzed more than 10 billion lines of code and found that companies and governments would need 61 billion workdays of software development time to pay off the technical debt they’ve accumulated over the past four decades.
A 2025 survey of 500+ IT professionals revealed that 62% of organizations still rely on legacy software systems.
Sonar’s research, based on an examination of over 200 projects, calculates that technical debt costs $306,000 per year for a project of one million lines of code — equivalent to 5,500 developer hours spent on remediation.
An OutSystems report found that 69% of IT leaders say technical debt fundamentally limits their ability to innovate.
The codebase I inherited wasn’t unique. It was typical. Built under deadline pressure by people who did the best they could with the time they had. Each shortcut made sense individually. Collectively, they’d created a system that nobody fully understood anymore.
That’s how legacy code is made. Not through malice. Through momentum.
What “10,000 Lines of Legacy Code” Actually Looks Like
I want to be specific about what I found, because vague descriptions of “messy code” aren’t useful.
The utils.js file (1,847 lines): No structure. Functions doing completely unrelated things sitting next to each other. A date formatting function, then a function that made an API call, then a function that manipulated DOM elements. All in one file with no explanation of why they were together.
The God Component (our main dashboard component, 892 lines): One React component. Contained local state for 14 different things. Made 6 API calls directly. Had 23 different conditional rendering branches. useEffect hooks that were 40 lines long. The component did everything — fetched data, processed it, formatted it, rendered it, and handled user interactions for the entire dashboard.
The Copied Logic: The same date formatting logic appeared in 7 different files. Slightly different in each one. When we found a bug in the original, it took a full sprint to find and fix all the copies.
The Dead Code: Functions that were never called. Components that were imported but not rendered. Feature flags for features that had been removed. Comments saying “TODO: remove this” with dates from two years prior.
The Magic Numbers:
if (score > 47) { ... }
setTimeout(callback, 3200)
const MAX = 15No explanation of where 47, 3200, or 15 came from. One of them turned out to be a business rule from a contract that had since changed. We’d been enforcing a contract term that no longer existed.
This is what 10,000 lines of accumulated legacy code looks like in practice. Not dramatic. Just gradually incomprehensible.
The Approach That Didn’t Kill Us
The number one mistake teams make with legacy code is deciding to rewrite it.
I know the rewrite is tempting. I’ve felt it. The code is a mess, the architecture is wrong, you know exactly how you’d do it better — just let me start fresh and in six months we’ll have something clean.
Six months later: the rewrite isn’t done, the old system is still running, you’ve now got two systems to maintain, and the new one has a whole new set of problems because you didn’t understand why the old one did some of the things it did.
Joel Spolsky called this “the single worst strategic mistake any software company can make.” He wrote it in 2000. Teams are still making it.
My approach: strangler fig pattern, incrementally.
The strangler fig pattern (named by Martin Fowler after a plant that grows around a tree and gradually replaces it) means you build new code around the old code, slowly replacing pieces while the old system keeps running. You never have a “big bang” rewrite moment. You have a hundred small replacement moments.
Here’s how I applied it:
Phase 1: Understand before you change (Weeks 1–2)
I didn’t write a single line of new code for two full weeks. I read. I traced function calls. I added log statements to understand the actual execution paths. I wrote down what the code did, not what it was supposed to do.
This is the most important and most skipped step. Developers want to fix code. Reading code feels passive, unproductive. But you cannot safely change what you don’t understand. The outgoing developer’s “don’t touch that file” advice wasn’t superstition — it was a warning that nobody had taken the time to understand it.
Phase 2: Write characterization tests before touching anything (Weeks 2–4)
A characterization test doesn’t test what the code should do. It tests what the code actually does right now.
// Not testing correctness - testing current behavior
test('formatUserScore returns 47 for input of 0.47', () => {
expect(formatUserScore(0.47)).toBe(47)
})test('formatUserScore returns 0 for null input', () => {
expect(formatUserScore(null)).toBe(0) // Even if this is "wrong"
})
This gave me a safety net. Before I changed anything, I had tests documenting the existing behavior. If my refactoring changed the output, the tests would catch it.
I went from 23% to ~45% test coverage just from characterization tests. Without writing a single new feature.
Phase 3: The actual refactoring (Months 2–4)
Small changes. One at a time. Never more than a few hundred lines per PR. Each change tested. Each change deployed and monitored before the next one.
The Specific Changes (And What They Taught Me)
Change 1: Breaking Apart the God Component
The 892-line dashboard component got broken into:

• useDashboardData — custom hook for all data fetching (moved 6 API calls here)

• DashboardFilters — filter controls (moved 3 local state pieces here)

• MetricCard — individual metric display (extracted from inline rendering)

• DashboardCharts — chart rendering section (extracted)

• DashboardTable — table section (extracted)

• Dashboard — the parent that composes everything (~80 lines)
What I learned: The God Component existed because it was easy to keep adding things to something that already worked. Every new requirement went into the same file because that’s where the data was. The solution isn’t just “make smaller components” — it’s creating a structure that makes the right place obvious. When you have a DashboardFilters component, the next developer adds filter logic there instead of to the parent.
Change 2: Eliminating the Duplicate Date Logic
Seven copies of date formatting. I extracted it into a single dateUtils.ts:
// dateUtils.ts - now the one true source of date formatting
export function formatDisplayDate(date: Date | string | null): string {
if (!date) return '—'
return new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-US', {
month: 'short',
day: 'numeric',
year: 'numeric'
}).format(new Date(date))
}export function formatRelativeTime(date: Date | string): string {
const diff = Date.now() - new Date(date).getTime()
const days = Math.floor(diff / 86400000)
if (days === 0) return 'today'
if (days === 1) return 'yesterday'
return `${days} days ago`
}
Then ran a find-and-replace across the codebase, replacing all 7 variations with imports from dateUtils.ts.
What I learned: Duplication is almost always the result of isolation. The developer who wrote the second copy didn’t see the first one. The fix isn’t just removing duplicates — it’s creating shared utilities and making them discoverable, so the next developer finds them instead of writing a third copy.
Change 3: Naming the Magic Numbers
// Before
if (score > 47) { ... }
setTimeout(callback, 3200)// After
const SCORE_THRESHOLD_FOR_PREMIUM_FEATURES = 47 // Set by product team Q2 2023, see ticket #1847
const ANIMATION_COMPLETE_DELAY_MS = 3200 // CSS transition is 3s, +200ms buffer
This took one afternoon. It was the highest ratio of value-to-effort change I made in four months.
What I learned: Magic numbers are documentation debt. Every unexplained number is a question future developers have to answer by reading git history, asking people, or guessing. Naming them costs almost nothing. Not naming them costs time and bugs.
Change 4: Deleting 3,000 Lines of Dead Code
This was terrifying. I was deleting code I didn’t fully understand in a system I was still learning.
My process:

• Find unused exports with TypeScript: error TS6133: 'handleLegacyAuth' is declared but its value is never read

• Search the entire codebase (including git history) for any reference

• If not referenced anywhere for 6+ months, delete with a comment in the PR explaining why

• Monitor production for 2 weeks after each deletion
I deleted:

• 847 lines of feature flag code for a feature that shipped 18 months ago (the flags were removed, the code wasn’t)

• 412 lines of a payment integration that had been replaced (the old integration was never cleaned up)

• 1,200+ lines of utility functions that TypeScript reported as unused

• Dozens of commented-out code blocks with dates from 2021–2022
What I learned: Deleted code is free code. It has no bugs, no security vulnerabilities, no maintenance cost. Developers are emotionally attached to code — “we might need it again!” — but git is a time machine. Nothing is truly deleted; it’s just moved to history. Delete aggressively.
Change 5: The utils.js Problem
I saved this for last deliberately. It was the most complex, the most risky, and the most educational.
My approach: move functions out of utils.js one at a time into domain-specific files.
utils.js (1,847 lines)
↓
dateUtils.ts (~80 lines)
apiHelpers.ts (~120 lines)
formatters.ts (~90 lines)
validators.ts (~110 lines)
domHelpers.ts (~60 lines)
[dead code deleted]Each move was a separate PR. Each PR got reviewed. Each got deployed and monitored.
After 6 weeks, utils.js was down to 47 lines — genuinely miscellaneous things that didn't belong anywhere else. I renamed it misc.ts and documented every function in it.
What I learned: The problem with a catch-all utils file isn't the file — it's the absence of a better home for things. When you create domain-specific homes (dateUtils, apiHelpers, formatters), things naturally sort themselves. But you have to create the homes first.
The Bugs I Found (The Unexpected Benefit)
Nobody told me that refactoring would find bugs. I expected it to improve the code. I didn’t expect to find things that were actively wrong.
Bug 1: The silent failure
While extracting API call logic, I noticed:
async function fetchUserData(userId) {
try {
const response = await api.get(`/users/${userId}`)
return response.data
} catch (error) {
console.log(error) // Logged but swallowed
return n
